newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs bigger lending rates cuts, ICICI head.
newsitem.headline: India needs bigger lending rates cuts, ICICI head.

text.p: India needs sharper cuts in lending rates to reverse sagging industrial growth, a top banker urged on Thursday, the day the country's biggest commercial bank announced a one percentage point cut in its prime rate.
"We have to give much sharper cuts than the 0.5 percent or 1.0 percent," Narayanan Vaghul, chairman of Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India Ltd (ICICI), said.
"I don't think that the industrial growth rate can be sustained with these high interest rates," he told a seminar on revitalising India's capital market.
On Thursday, the State Bank of India (SBI) said it had decided to cut its prime lending rate to 14.5 percent from 15.5 percent with effect from November 1.
Other banks have also lowered the rates in the past few days with many more expected to follow suit.
State-run term lending institutions, including ICICI, on Wednesday reduced their prime rates by 0.50 percentage point to 17 percent.

The cuts were sparked by easier liquidity constraints enshrined in the central bank's monetary policy for the second half of 1996/97 (April-March) announced on Saturday to jump-start a slowing economy.
Industrial production in June 1996, the latest month for which government figures are available, grew 6.8 percent year-on-year compared to 10.6 percent in May and 12.2 percent a year ago.
The prime rate is what banks charge their blue-chip clients. Following the latest cuts, it varies between 14.5 and 19.0 percent. Other borrowers have to pay more.
Vaghul said companies had put off expansion and diversification plans and diverted internal cash accruals to fund working capital requirements to beat high interest rates.
"I'm looking at (a) real prime rate target of five to six percent (per annum)," he told Reuters after addressing the seminar.
The real rate is exclusive of inflation, which currently is about 7.0 percent as measured by the wholesale price index.
"There's no recession, only a slight slowdown," said Hemendra Kothari, chairman of DSP Merrill Lynch Financial Consultants. "The lending rate must substantially come down."

Vaghul said banks, term lending institutions and private finance firms must jointly set an agenda to tackle the high rates problem by eschewing the race to lure deposits by offering high interest rates.
"The RBI (Reserve Bank of India) has given a signal to lower interest rates," he said. "The ball is now in our court."
